In-house residential homes alone are £380k over budget (up £205k since Q1). These pressures are being masked by £1.051m in staff vacancies that will close as posts are filled. The service notes this investment (front-door staffing) should reduce long-term costs, but creates a near-term cliff.
findings.matters: CLA placement costs are among the fastest-growing pressures in children's services nationally. Powys's placement inflation plus complexity suggests aging stock of higher-need children. Staff vacancies masking costs is unsustainable. When these posts fill, the overspend will surface unless placements reduce.
findings.figures: £1.764m CLA placement pressures; £306k increase since Q1; £380k in-house residential overspend; £1.051m staffing underspend masking issues
findings.quote: £1.764 million Children Looked After (CLA) placements, Adoption & SGO's. This includes £905,000 of required placement savings for the Fostering Framework Invest to Save project... An increase of £306,000 since quarter 1... All baseline budget underspends of £1.628 million are currently being utilised to mitigate the overall budget forecast overspend.

findings.headline: General Fund Reserve is at the minimum policy threshold of 4.2% with only £0.8m underspend forecast, leaving no buffer for emerging pressures
findings.detail: The council's General Fund Reserve stands at £11.4m, representing 4.2% of net revenue budget. The policy requires a minimum of 4%. With only £0.8m overall underspend forecasted and £12.5m of specifically held reserves planned to be drawn down during the year, there is no safety margin if cost pressures materialise. Schools are also increasing their reserve draw from £1.6m to £2.2m.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know a council has financial buffers for unexpected pressures. Powys has none. Any deviation from the forecast would require either emergency savings, service cuts, or a breach of policy. Reserves fell from £71.5m to projected £58.9m.
findings.figures: General Fund Reserve £11.4m (4.2% of budget); policy minimum 4%; overall useable reserves falling from £61.9m to £55.3m; schools reserve draw increasing to £2.2m
findings.quote: The General Fund reserve at £11.4 million, the equivalent of 4.2% of the net revenue budget for 2025 (excluding schools delegated budgets and the HRA). The Council's Reserves policy requires the General Fund Reserve to be maintained at a minimum of 4% of net revenue budget.

findings.headline: £1.3m of cost reductions (8% of total) are unachieved and at risk of delivery in this year with no disclosed remedial plan
findings.detail: The council approved £16.0m of cost reductions to balance 2025-26 (including £3.7m rolled forward from prior years). By Q2, only 60.7% (£9.7m) have been delivered and 30.9% (£4.9m) are assured. The remaining £1.3m are explicitly unachieved and at risk. The report states that services must 'consider what remedial action they take' but identifies no plan. If these are not recovered, alternative funding will be required mid-year.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver agreed savings would force either emergency cuts or further reserve drawdowns on a council already at minimum reserves. It indicates the baseline budget is not genuinely sustainable.
findings.figures: £1.3 million (8.0%) unachieved; £16.0 million total cost reductions required; 60.7% delivery rate
findings.quote: £1.3 million (8.0%) are described as unachieved and are at risk of delivery in this year. Those services that show unachieved cost reductions must consider what remedial action they take to mitigate the impact on the overall performance within their service as their budget forecast must come back to a balanced position.

findings.headline: Virgin Media legal case disclosed as contingent liability relating to members' pension benefits, with financial impact unquantified
findings.detail: A contingent liability has been added to the accounts relating to a Virgin Media legal case affecting members' pension benefits. The nature and potential cost of this liability are not disclosed in the audit report.
findings.matters: Unquantified pension-related liabilities represent a crystallisation risk that could materially increase the council's pension deficit or require reserve drawdown if the legal outcome is unfavourable.
findings.figures: Amount unquantified
findings.quote: Contingent Liability narrative note added in relation to the impact of the Virgin Media legal case in relation to changes made to members' pension benefits

findings.headline: New finance system goes live 1 April 2026 with the current system becoming unavailable after July 2026, covering the entire 2025-26 audit window and creating a critical deadline risk
findings.detail: The council is implementing a new finance system from April 2026 while the old system ends in July 2026. This creates a high-pressure period where the council must close its 2025-26 accounts during or immediately after the system switchover, while also meeting an audit deadline being brought forward to September 2026. The auditor emphasises this timeline creates execution risk and that audit quality depends on receiving fully prepared, high-quality accounts and working papers upfront.
findings.matters: Finance system implementations are operationally high-risk; a failed transition or delayed system availability directly impacts the council's ability to close accounts on time and could cascade into audit delays that affect financial reporting timelines and borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: Old system unavailable: July 2026; audit deadline: September 2026
findings.quote: This will be particularly important for the Council given the planned implementation of a new finance system from 01 April 2026 and the current system not being available after July 2026 (the whole of the 2025-26 audit window).

findings.headline: Schools Reserve became overspent in 2024-25, requiring management action to address the deficit
findings.detail: The auditor has highlighted that the Schools Reserve became overspent during the financial year. A footnote was added to the accounts documenting this and noting what management is doing to resolve it. The specific overspend amount is not stated in this report.
findings.matters: A major service area losing budget control signals management capability issues and forces the council to use other reserves or reallocate resources to cover the shortfall.
findings.figures: Overspend amount not disclosed in this report
findings.quote: A footnote has been added to comment on the Schools Reserve becoming overspent in the year and what is being done to address it.

findings.headline: Very few officers have received risk management training since the programme was relaunched in mid-2024
findings.detail: The council relaunched risk management training in mid-2024 but uptake among officers and Members has been very low. The council recognises it has more to do to identify key roles and provide targeted training. Effective training is necessary to ensure staff understand their risk management responsibilities.
findings.matters: Skills gaps in risk management at operational level could impair the council's ability to identify and escalate emerging financial or operational risks early.
findings.figures: Training relaunched mid-2024; uptake described as 'very few'
findings.quote: Since relaunching its risk management training in mid-2024, very few officers have attended. The Council recognises that it has more to do to identify key roles and to upskill officers through targeted training.

findings.headline: Risk and performance reporting are separated, obscuring linkages between risk, budget and service performance
findings.detail: The Cabinet receives separate quarterly reports on performance, budget monitoring and risk. The performance report does not refer to relevant strategic risks, meaning connections between financial pressures, service performance and identified risks may not be clearly visible to decision-makers.
findings.matters: Separated reporting of risk and performance can mask financial stress; a lender needs confidence that emerging financial problems are being surfaced visibly to the council's leadership.
findings.figures: Reports issued quarterly
findings.quote: The Cabinet receive separate performance, budget monitoring and risk reports every quarter. The performance report does not refer to relevant strategic risks. This means that the linkages between risk, performance and budget may not always be clear in all instances.

findings.headline: Controls marked complete but reasons for remaining on risk register unclear, suggesting weak monitoring
findings.detail: Progress statements in the risk register do not consistently align to documented controls and actions. Many controls are marked as complete yet it remains unclear why those risks remain on the register, meaning the register summaries activity rather than demonstrating the impact of actual risk controls.
findings.matters: If the council cannot clearly articulate why managed risks remain active, it signals weak monitoring of control effectiveness; the council may not detect when mitigations fail.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided
findings.quote: Those statements do not consistently align to the controls and actions. Many controls or actions are marked as complete, and it is unclear why the those remain on the register. The register therefore summarises activity rather than providing evidence of the impact of risk controls.

findings.headline: Risk mitigation actions lack clear specification and costs, preventing assessment of effectiveness
findings.detail: The council sets out controls and mitigating actions in its risk register but these are not consistently SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Timebound) nor are they costed. This means the council cannot assess whether its mitigation spending is achieving the intended impact or how to allocate resources most effectively.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on reported risk reductions if the council cannot demonstrate the actions taken are effective; spending on risk mitigation may not be translating to genuine risk reduction.
findings.figures: No specific figures on cost of mitigation actions provided
findings.quote: The Council sets out controls or actions in its risk register, however those are not always SMART nor costed. This means that the Council is not able to assess the effectiveness of the actions it is taking, properly monitor progress, or determine how best to allocate resources.

findings.headline: Most of the council's fifteen strategic risks exceeded its agreed risk appetite in late 2024
findings.detail: The council has defined risk appetite and tolerance levels but does not clearly communicate them in its strategic risk register. In late 2024, most of the fifteen risks on the strategic register exceeded the council's agreed risk appetite, but the audit found the rationale for carrying these risks was unclear, suggesting the council was not actively managing risks to target levels.
findings.matters: Risks exceeding risk appetite while management rationale is unclear indicates the council's control environment may be weaker than intended; a lender needs to know that identified risks are being actively managed to acceptable levels.
findings.figures: 15 strategic risks; most exceeded agreed appetite as of late 2024
findings.quote: In late 2024, most of the fifteen strategic risks on its register exceeded the Council's agreed risk appetite. However, because the Council had not clearly communicated its risk appetite and tolerance levels, the rationale for carrying these risks was unclear.

findings.paper_title: 1 Q1 Treasury Management Report GAC Sept 2025
findings.headline: PWLB borrowing remains prohibited for Powys, restricting access to the cheapest form of local authority borrowing and forcing higher costs if future capital strategy includes asset purchases for yield.
findings.detail: A standing prohibition denies PWLB access to any authority with asset-for-yield schemes in its capital programme. Powys currently has none. However, the council explicitly flags that if it pursues such schemes in future, it will lose PWLB access and 'borrowing sources other than the PWLB are likely to be more expensive.' This is material given the forecast capital financing requirement reaching £612.4m by March 2028.
findings.matters: PWLB restriction creates hidden cost inflation for any future asset-led regeneration or yield strategy, reducing financial flexibility and imposing higher revenue costs if capital strategy shifts.
findings.figures: Current CFR forecast £612.4 million by 31 March 2028; zero asset-for-yield schemes in current programme
findings.quote: With the significant amounts of borrowing in the future Capital Programme, the inability to access PWLB borrowing will need to be a major consideration for any future purchases of assets for yield. The additional income these assets generate must be sufficient to cover the increased borrowing costs, as borrowing sources other than the PWLB are likely to be more expensive.

findings.paper_title: 1 Q1 Treasury Management Report GAC Sept 2025
findings.headline: Council tax collection fell to 26.69% (down year-on-year) with prior-year arrears of £8.49 million swollen by a self-catering reclassification that triggered valuation appeals.
findings.detail: In-year council tax collection rate fell to 26.69% by end June 2025, down 0.15 percentage points compared to same point in 2024/25. Uncollected prior-year council tax jumped significantly to £8.49m. The spike stems from 270 self-catering units reclassified from business rates to council tax in 2024/25 with a 75% premium (175% total council tax charge), budgeted to generate £2.5m additional revenue. However, many bills exceed £10,000 and are facing appeals to the Valuation Office Agency, creating collection uncertainty.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates and rising arrears reduce cash inflow and increase borrowing dependence. Valuation appeals are protracted, delaying and potentially preventing collection of material sums.
findings.figures: £8.49 million prior-year council tax arrears; 26.69% in-year collection rate (down 0.15%); 270 units reclassified; £2.5 million additional budgeted revenue; 75% premium per unit
findings.quote: £8.49 million of Council Tax... remains uncollected from previous financial years. The Council tax figure has increased significantly compared to that reported last year... collection is challenging as many are appealing the decision with the Valuation Office Agency.

findings.paper_title: 1 Q1 Treasury Management Report GAC Sept 2025
findings.headline: Aged sundry debt jumped by £1.6 million in Q1 to £14.77 million, entirely from PTHB (social care) owing to Welsh Government collection restrictions.
findings.detail: Aged debt over 30 days increased from £13.17m at end March to £14.77m by 7 July. Of this, 72% (£8.4m) is social care debt. PTHB aged debt alone rose by £1.61m in the quarter. The council acknowledges the debt is 'challenging to collect' because Welsh Government restricts use of bailiffs for residential care fees and repayment often depends on selling properties or settling estates. The council has committed to a September 2025 deadline to clear prioritised debt and is exploring hiring a dedicated solicitor for enforcement.
findings.matters: Rising uncollected debt creates working capital pressure, requiring increased borrowing or reserve drawdown. Growth entirely in social care suggests underlying billing or service delivery issues, not temporary collection lag.
findings.figures: £14.77 million aged debt (over 30 days); £1.6 million increase in Q1; £8.4 million (72%) social care debt; £1.61 million from PTHB alone; collection rate 56% in June
findings.quote: The level of aged debt (over 30 days old) has increased by £1.60 million since the last quarter... PTHB aged debt against the previous quarter has increased by £1.61 million. We are working together to prioritise and clear the aged debt with a deadline of September 2025.
